opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the ones I use most are pretty unglamorous. Coding assistants are probably number one. I write a lot of code, and having something that can draft a function, explain an unfamiliar codebase, or catch a dumb bug before I spend twenty minutes staring at it has changed how I work day to day. It's not that it writes everything for me. It removes a lot of the friction between having an idea and testing it.

Second would be general-purpose chat models for thinking things through. I use them almost like a sparring partner. If I'm reading a paper, I'll ask it to poke holes in the argument, or I'll describe an approach I'm considering and ask what could go wrong. It's not always right, but it's fast, it's available at two in the morning, and it often surfaces something I hadn't considered.

Then there's research and search. Being able to ask a question and get a synthesized answer with sources, rather than opening fifteen tabs, saves a surprising amount of time, especially when I'm getting up to speed on a new area.

What I'm most excited about, though, and what I don't think anyone has fully nailed yet, are applications that actually *do* things over longer horizons. Not just answering a question, but taking a goal, planning, executing across many steps, and coming back with a result you can trust. Today's tools are great copilots. The step change comes when they become reliable agents you can delegate real work to. That's a big part of why I find this moment so interesting.

r001.rationale: The response lists coding assistants, chat models, and research tools as useful now, and describes longer-horizon agents as a future advance. It does not characterize the current tools as invisible background systems or explicitly judge them more useful than AGI-like applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing I use most every day is just the frontier chat models themselves, and more and more, the coding agents built on top of them. I spend a lot of time writing and reviewing code, and having something that can take a vague description of what I want, scaffold it, run the tests, and come back with a working first pass has genuinely changed how I work. It's not that it does everything perfectly, it's that the loop between having an idea and seeing whether it works has collapsed from hours to minutes.

The second thing is research. If I'm trying to get up to speed on a paper or a technique outside my immediate area, I'll have a long back-and-forth with a model where I push on it, ask it to explain the intuition, try to find holes in it. It's like having a very patient colleague who has read everything, even if they occasionally misremember a detail, so you still have to check.

And then there's a category that I think is underrated, which is just the boring stuff. Drafting emails, summarizing a long thread I got CC'd on, turning rough notes into something I can actually send to someone. None of that is glamorous, but it adds up to a lot of time back in the week.

What I find interesting is that the applications I find most useful are the ones where the model is embedded in a workflow and can actually take actions, rather than just answer questions. That's where I think most of the value over the next couple of years is going to come from. The chat interface was the demo. The agent that sits in your tools and does the work is the product.

r001.rationale: The candidate favors chat models, coding agents, research, and routine tasks, but does not compare invisible background AI systems with AGI-like applications or say the former are more useful now.

astra-6.text: For me, coding is probably the most useful application right now. You have this very fast feedback loop: you ask for something, run the code, and see whether it works. I also find AI useful as a thought partner—taking an idea, asking it to challenge my assumptions, or getting an explanation of something unfamiliar. You still need to check what it tells you, but it can make that process much faster.

r001.rationale: The response identifies coding and thought-partner uses as helpful, but does not compare invisible background AI systems with AGI-like applications or say which is more useful.
